name: olsrd
desc: Implementation of the optimized link state routing protocol
why: A working implementation of the OLSR mesh routing protocol, a door into how self-organizing networks find their own paths.

brief.what_it_is: olsrd is the olsr.org Optimized Link-State Routing daemon, version 1 of the OLSR routing protocol. It runs on a machine and exchanges link-state information with neighboring nodes so that the machine can pick paths through a mesh network. The olsr.org site describes it as a routing daemon for mobile ad hoc networks on embedded devices such as commercial off-the-shelf routers, smartphones, or ordinary computers. The fetched README is mostly license text and does not spell out inputs and outputs, so the detail here comes from the project website.
brief.why_it_exists: The project implements the IETF MANET group's Optimized Link State Routing Protocol (RFC 3626) for self-organizing wireless mesh networks. Per olsr.org, it began as a 2004 Master Thesis by Andreas Tonnesen and was later used by Freifunk, FunkFeuer and others to build community mesh networks.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the mechanism. The olsr.org site says olsrd is a link-state protocol optimized for mobile ad hoc networks, and that olsrd2 is a rewrite built on the OONF framework that follows RFC 6130 (neighborhood discovery) and RFC 7181 (OLSRv2). Nothing in the pages I read describes the internals of olsrd v1 beyond that.
brief.install_notes: The README gives no build or install steps. The repository has a Makefile and Makefile.inc at the top level, plus debian, redhat, openbsd and android directories, so packaging exists for those platforms. The README-LINUX_NL80211.txt file in the repo suggests Linux wireless setup is covered there, but I did not fetch it. The brew install is the only route I confirmed.
brief.standout: It is a long-lived, real-world mesh routing daemon with packaging for Debian, Red Hat, OpenBSD and Android. Its origin is a master's thesis that grew into a community-network tool. Its successor olsrd2 is a full rewrite on a separate framework, so this repo is the older branch.
brief.status: Maintained, per the GitHub About text, which says it is maintained by Freifunk Berlin. The repo shows 6,139 commits, 95 stars, 71 forks, and a .github/workflows directory with CI. I could not see a last-commit or release date on the fetched page, so the exact recency is unknown.
brief.caveats: This is olsrd v1. The olsr.org site points to olsrd2 as the successor, and this entry should not be read as the newest implementation. The README is almost entirely the BSD-style license text, with no quickstart. The repo says the nmealib library in the PUD plugin is LGPL. The fetched material gives no build instructions, so the install path beyond brew is unverified.

olsrd and olsrd2 are both Link State Routing Protocol implementations optimized for Mobile ad hoc networks on embedded devices like commercial of the shelf routers, smartphones or normal computers.
The development of the implementation was continued in an open source project as the routing protocol was used by Freifunk, FunkFeuer and others to build Community Mesh Networks.

judge.reason: A working mesh-routing daemon is a hands-on way to explore how self-organizing wireless networks discover neighbors and choose paths.

entry.title: olsrd
entry.tldr: A routing daemon from community wireless mesh networks, where each node learns its neighbours and works out paths through the network with no central router.
entry.deeper_look:
olsrd is the olsr.org implementation of the Optimized Link State Routing Protocol, version 1 (RFC 3626, from the IETF MANET group). Each machine running it swaps link-state information with its neighbours and uses that to choose paths across a mesh. The olsr.org site describes it as built for mobile ad hoc networks on embedded devices "like commercial of the shelf routers, smartphones or normal computers."

It began as a 2004 Master Thesis by Andreas Tonnesen. It then grew into an open source project because, in the project's words, "the routing protocol was used by Freifunk, FunkFeuer and others to build Community Mesh Networks." The GitHub page says it is now maintained by Freifunk Berlin.

The idea underneath is a network that has no fixed topology and no one in charge. Nodes appear, vanish and move, and the routing tables have to keep up. Link-state routing is one answer to that problem, and reading about how olsrd handles it is a way into mesh networking in general.

The README is mostly license text, so expect to get your bearings from the olsr.org site and the repository's directories instead.
entry.install:
brew install olsrd
# A routing daemon normally needs root and a wireless interface. A real mesh needs more than one node, and the brief confirmed no setup steps beyond brew.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the daemon's command-line options, which is the quickest way to see what it can be told to do.

entry.whats_unique: It is a long-lived, real-world mesh routing daemon that community networks such as Freifunk and FunkFeuer have used, and it started as a master's thesis. Packaging exists for Debian, Red Hat, OpenBSD and Android.
entry.caveats: This is olsrd v1, the older branch; olsr.org points to olsrd2 as the successor, and the README has no quickstart, so setup details are unverified.
